title: God’s Sabbath is not a tired workman’s rest
source_text: Εἶτα πάλιν μὴ κατακούσας τοῦ „καὶ συνετέλεσεν ὁ θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἕκτῃ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ, ἃ ἐποίησε· καὶ κατέπαυσεν ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ, ὧν ἐποίησε. καὶ εὐλόγησεν ὁ θεὸς τὴν ἡμέραν τὴν ἑβδόμην καὶ ἡγίασεν αὐτὴν, ὅτι ἐν αὐτῇ κατέπαυσεν ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ, ὧν ἤρξατο ὁ θεὸς ποιῆσαι“ καὶ οἰηθεὶς ταὐτὸν εἶναι τὸ „κατέπαυσε τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ“ καὶ τὸ „ἀνεπαύσατο τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ“ φησί· μετὰ τοῦτο μὴν ὥσπερ τις ἀτεχνῶς πονηρὸς χειροτέχνης ἐκκαμὼν καὶ πρὸς ἀνάπαυσιν ἀργίας δεηθείς. οὐδὲ γὰρ οἶδε, τίς ἡ μετὰ τὴν ὅσον ὁ κόσμος συνέστηκεν ἐνεργουμένην κοσμοποιΐαν, ἡ τοῦ σαββάτου καὶ τῆς καταπαύσεως τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμέρα, ἐν ᾗ ἑορτάσουσιν ἅμα τῷ θεῷ οἱ πάντα τὰ ἔργα ἑαυτῶν ταῖς ἓξ ἡμέραις πεποιηκότες καὶ διὰ τὸ μηδὲν παραλελοιπέναι τῶν ἐπιβαλλόντων ἀναβαίνοντες ἐπὶ τὴν θεωρίαν καὶ τὴν ἐν αὐτῇ τῶν δικαίων καὶ μακαρίων πανήγυριν. εἶτα ὡς ἤτοι τῶν γραφῶν οὕτω λεγουσῶν ἢ καὶ ἡμῶν αὐτῶν οὕτως διηγουμένων περὶ θεοῦ, ὅτι καμὼν ἀνεπαύσατο, φησὶν ὅτι οὐ θέμις τὸν πρῶτον θεὸν κάμνειν οὔτε χειρουργεῖν οὔτε κελεύειν. ὁ μὲν οὖν Κέλσος φησὶν ὅτι οὐ θέμις τὸν πρῶτον θεὸν κάμνειν· ἡμεῖς δὲ εἴποιμεν ἂν ὅτι οὐδ᾿ ὁ θεὸς λόγος κάμνει οὐδ᾿ ὅσοι τῆς κρείττονος ἤδη καὶ θειοτέρας τάξεως ἔχονται· τὸ γὰρ κάμνειν ἐστὶ τῶν ἐν σώματι. ζητήσεις δὲ, πότερον ἢ τῶν ἐν οἱῳποτοῦν σώματι ἢ τῶν ἐν τῷ γηΐνῳ καὶ ὀλίγον τούτου βελτίονι. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ θέμις τὸν πρῶτον θεὸν χειρουργεῖν· ἐὰν δὲ κυρίως ἀκούῃς τοῦ χειρουργεῖν, οὐδὲ τὸν δεύτερον οὐδ᾿ ἄλλο τι τῶν θειοτέρων. ἀλλ᾿ ἔστω καταχρηστικῶς λέγεσθαι τὸ χειρουργεῖν ἢ τροπικῶς, ἵνα διηγησώμεθα καὶ τὸ „ποίησιν δὲ χειρῶν αὐτοῦ ἀναγγέλλει τὸ στερέωμα“ καὶ „αἱ χεῖρες αὐτοῦ ἔστησαν τὸν οὐρανὸν“ καὶ εἴ τι τούτοις εἴρηται παραπλησίως, τροπολογούντων ἡμῶν χεῖρας καὶ μέλη τοῦ θεοῦ· τί οὖν ἄτοπον οὕτω χειρουργεῖν θεόν; ὡς οὐκ ἄτοπον δὲ οὕτω χειρουργεῖν θεὸν, οὕτως οὐδὲ τὸ κελεύειν αὐτὸν, ἵνα καλὰ καὶ ἐπαινετὰ ᾖ τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ κελευομένου ἐπιτελούμενα τῷ θεὸν εἶναι τὸν κεκελευκότα περὶ αὐτῶν.
pass_a_gloss: Then again not hearing rightly (κατακούω) ‘and God finished (συντελέω) on the sixth day his works (ἔργα) which he made; and he ceased (καταπαύω) on the seventh day from all his works which he made; and God blessed (εὐλογέω) the seventh day and sanctified (ἁγιάζω) it, because on it he ceased from all his works which God began to make’, and supposing ‘ceased on the seventh day’ to be the same as ‘rested (ἀναπαύομαι) on the seventh day’, he says: ‘after this indeed, like some downright (ἀτεχνῶς) bad hand-worker (χειροτέχνης), worn out (ἐκκάμνω) and needing idleness (ἀργία) for rest (ἀνάπαυσις)’. For he does not know what is, after the world-making (κοσμοποιΐα) worked as long as the world stands, the day of the Sabbath (σάββατον) and of God’s rest (κατάπαυσις), on which those who have done all their works in the six days will keep feast (ἑορτάζω) together with God, and through having left aside nothing of what was incumbent (ἐπιβάλλω), ascend to the contemplation (θεωρία) and to the festal assembly (πανήγυρις) in it of the righteous (δίκαιοι) and blessed (μακάριοι). Then, as if either the Scriptures say so or we ourselves narrate (διηγέομαι) so about God, that having wearied (κάμνω) he rested, he says that it is not lawful (οὐ θέμις) for the first God to weary nor to work with hands (χειρουργέω) nor to command (κελεύω). Celsus says it is not lawful for the first God to weary; we would say that neither God the Word wearies nor those who hold already to the better and more divine order (τάξις); for wearying belongs to those in a body. You will seek whether [to those] in any body whatever or in the earthly and one a little better than this. But neither is it lawful for the first God to work with hands; and if you hear ‘work with hands’ properly (κυρίως), not the second either nor any other of the more divine [beings]. But let ‘working with hands’ be said by misuse (καταχρηστικῶς) or by trope (τροπικῶς), so that we may explain also ‘the firmament announces (ἀναγγέλλω) the making (ποίησις) of his hands’ and ‘his hands set (ἵστημι) the heaven’ and whatever is said like these, us figuring (τροπολογέω) hands and limbs (μέλη) of God; what then is absurd for God so to work with hands? As it is not absurd so for God to work with hands, so neither to command, so that the things accomplished (ἐπιτελέω) by the one commanded may be good and praiseworthy (ἐπαινετά) by the commander about them being God.
pass_b_english: Then again, having misheard the words: “And God finished on the sixth day His works which He had made; and He ceased on the seventh day from all His works which He had made. And God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it He ceased from all His works which God had begun to make” (Genesis 2:2–3), and supposing that “He ceased on the seventh day” is the same as “He rested on the seventh day,” he says: “After this, indeed, like a downright bad workman, worn out and in need of idleness to rest.”

For he does not know what the day of the Sabbath and of God’s rest is, the day that comes after the making of the world, a making carried on for as long as the world stands. On that day those who have done all their works in the six days will keep festival together with God (compare Hebrews 4:9–10), those who, because they have left undone nothing of what fell to them, go up to contemplation and to the festal gathering of the righteous and blessed held on that day (compare Hebrews 12:22–23).

Then, as if either the Scriptures said so or we ourselves explained it so concerning God, that He grew weary and rested, he says: “It is not right for the first God to grow weary, nor to work with His hands, nor to give commands.” Celsus, then, says that it is not right for the first God to grow weary. But we would say that neither does God the Word grow weary, nor do any who already belong to the better and more divine order; for growing weary belongs to beings in a body. You may ask whether it belongs to those in a body of any kind whatever, or to those in an earthly body and one a little better than this.

But neither is it right for the first God to work with His hands; and if you take “work with the hands” in its proper sense, neither is it right for the second, nor for any other of the more divine beings. But let “working with the hands” be said loosely or figuratively, so that we may explain also: “The firmament proclaims the work of His hands” (Psalm 19:1), and: “His hands set up the heaven” (compare Isaiah 45:12), and anything said like these, when we take the hands and limbs of God figuratively. What, then, is absurd in God’s working with His hands in this way? And as it is not absurd for God to work with His hands in this way, so neither is it absurd for Him to give commands, so that the things carried out by the one commanded may be good and praiseworthy because the one who gave the command about them is God.

choices.choice: Genesis 2:2 LXX reads ‘on the sixth day’ where the Hebrew has ‘seventh’; Origen’s text follows the LXX and is kept. Origen’s point turns on the difference between κατέπαυσε (‘ceased’, the LXX verb) and ἀνεπαύσατο (‘rested’, i.e. took a rest after fatigue), so ‘ceased’ and ‘rested’ are kept distinct. Psalm 19:1 is LXX Psalm 18:2. ‘His hands set up the heaven’ matches no LXX verse exactly; the nearest are Isaiah 45:12 (‘with my hand I made the heaven firm’) and Isaiah 48:13 (‘my right hand made the heaven firm’); cited as an allusion. The Sabbath-rest and festal-gathering language is not a quotation but recalls Hebrews 4:9–10 and 12:22–23 (πανήγυρις, ‘the righteous’); cited with ‘compare’. In τὴν ἐν αὐτῇ … πανήγυριν, αὐτῇ may refer to the day (as rendered) or to the contemplation (‘the festal gathering within it’). ἀναβαίνοντες is a present participle describing the same people, so ‘go up’ is kept in the present. ‘The second’ (τὸν δεύτερον) means the second God, i.e. the Word, in Origen’s usage against Celsus’s ‘first God’; left as Origen phrases it. Celsus’s fragment ‘After this, indeed, like a downright bad workman…’ is incomplete in Origen’s citation and is kept so; ἀτεχνῶς (‘downright’) may carry a play on ἄτεχνος, ‘unskilled’.
